# Combination GLP-1 receptor agonist and SGLT2 inhibitor therapy versus GLP-1 receptor agonist monotherapy on arrhythmia outcomes in non-diabetic obese patients: A real-world time-dependent analysis

**Authors:** George A. Blankson; Irene A. Acheampong; Abraham K. Carboo; Dennis D. Kumi; Joseph Amoah; Abdi Nawal; Stephen Nii-Ashie Djanie; Isaac Prempeh; Adama Seidu; Richmond K.E. Buckner

**Affiliations:** aDepartment of Internal Medicine, Case Western Reserve University/University Hospitals Cleveland Medical Center, Cleveland, OH, USA | bDepartment of Medicine, Clinical Research Unit, Carilion Clinic, Roanoke, VA, USA | cDepartment of Internal Medicine, University of Connecticut School of Medicine, Farmington, CT, USA | dDepartment of Cardiology, University of Illinois College of Medicine at Peoria, Peoria, IL, USA | eDepartment of Cardiology, Case Western Reserve University/University Hospitals Cleveland Medical Center, Cleveland, OH, USA | fDepartment of Medicine, Cayuga Medical Center, Ithaca, NY, USA | gDepartment of Medicine, UNC Health Blue Ridge Hospital, Morganton, NC, USA | hDepartment of Internal Medicine, Woodhull Medical and Mental Health Center, Brooklyn, NY, USA | iDepartment of Internal Medicine, Loyola University Health System, MacNeal Hospital, Berwyn, IL, USA

## Abstract

Glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonists (GLP-1RA) and sodium-glucose cotransporter-2 inhibitors (SGLT2i) have established cardiometabolic benefits and are increasingly used in combination, including in patients without diabetes. Although both drug classes have been studied extensively for metabolic and cardiovascular outcomes, their effects on cardiac arrhythmias, particularly in non-diabetic obese patients, remain poorly defined.

To compare arrhythmia outcomes in non-diabetic obese patients receiving combined GLP-1RA and SGLT2i therapy versus GLP-1RA alone, with particular focus on time-dependent changes in atrial and ventricular arrhythmia risk.

We performed a retrospective real-world cohort study of non-diabetic obese adults treated with either combined GLP-1RA and SGLT2i therapy or GLP-1RA alone. Cohorts were balanced through propensity score matching. The primary outcome was composite arrhythmia. Secondary outcomes included atrial fibrillation/flutter, ventricular tachycardia, and ventricular fibrillation. Outcomes were assessed at 60 months, with additional longitudinal analyses from 6 months through 96 months to better define the timing of benefit and the evolution of arrhythmia risk.

At 60 months, combination therapy was associated with 17.5% lower odds of composite arrhythmia compared with GLP-1RA alone, OR 0.825 (0.731-0.932). This benefit emerged by 24 months and persisted through 96 months. The reduction in the primary outcome was driven mainly by lower atrial arrhythmia burden, with atrial fibrillation/flutter occurring 17.9% less often in the combination group at 60 months, OR 0.821 (0.722-0.934); this benefit became apparent by 18 months and remained present through 96 months. In contrast, ventricular tachycardia was more frequent in the combination group during earlier follow-up intervals, including 6, 12, 18, and 24 months, but this difference was not sustained and became similar between groups around 60 months, OR 1.186 (0.943-1.491), and persisted through 96 months. Ventricular fibrillation remained comparable between groups throughout the follow-up period.

In non-diabetic obese patients, combined GLP-1RA and SGLT2i therapy was associated with lower long-term odds of composite arrhythmia compared with GLP-1RA alone, largely driven by a reduction in atrial fibrillation/flutter. An increased ventricular tachycardia risk with combination therapy appeared to diminish over time, while ventricular fibrillation remained unchanged. These findings suggest that combination therapy may have a favorable long-term electrophysiologic profile in non-diabetic obesity and highlight the importance of time-dependent analysis when evaluating arrhythmia outcomes with cardiometabolic therapies.

## Introduction

Obesity is a major global health problem and is strongly associated with cardiovascular disease, including cardiac arrhythmias such as atrial fibrillation (AF). The risk of arrhythmias in obesity is driven by structural and electrical remodeling, inflammation, and autonomic imbalance. As obesity rates continue to rise, understanding how modern therapies affect arrhythmia risk has become increasingly important [1,2].

Glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonists (GLP-1RAs) and sodium-glucose cotransporter-2 inhibitors (SGLT2i) were initially developed for type 2 diabetes but have demonstrated important cardiovascular benefits beyond glucose control. GLP-1 RAs reduce major adverse cardiovascular events, while SGLT2i consistently reduce heart failure hospitalizations and improve renal outcomes [[3], [4], [5], [6]]. More recently, GLP-1RAs have shown significant weight loss and cardiovascular benefit in non-diabetic individuals with obesity, and SGLT2i have demonstrated benefits in heart failure and chronic kidney disease regardless of diabetes status [[7], [8], [9], [10]].

The effects of these medications on cardiac arrhythmias are less well defined. GLP-1RAs have generally demonstrated a neutral to modestly favorable arrhythmia profile, with meta-analyses showing no increased risk of atrial or ventricular arrhythmias and some studies reporting reductions in incident AF, particularly with semaglutide [[11], [12], [13], [14]]. In contrast, SGLT2i have been more consistently associated with reductions in atrial arrhythmias, including AF and atrial flutter, although their effects on ventricular arrhythmias such as ventricular tachycardia (VT) and ventricular fibrillation (VF) appear largely neutral [[15], [16], [17], [18]].

Combination therapy with GLP-1RAs and SGLT2i is increasingly used because of complementary metabolic and cardiovascular effects, with prior studies suggesting additive benefits in weight loss and cardiometabolic risk reduction [19,20]. However, data on arrhythmia outcomes with combination therapy is scarce. In addition, the timing of arrhythmia benefits after initiation of therapy is not well defined. The objective of this study is to compare arrhythmia outcomes in non-diabetic obese patients treated with combined GLP-1RA and SGLT2i therapy versus GLP-1RA monotherapy. We hypothesized that combination therapy would be associated with a lower risk of overall arrhythmias, due to the complementary cardiometabolic effects of both drug classes. We also sought to characterize the temporal evolution of arrhythmia risk by evaluating outcomes across multiple follow-up intervals from 6 months through 96 months.

## Methods

### Data source

Data were obtained from the TriNetX Analytics Network, a large U.S.-based multicenter federated health research network aggregating de-identified electronic health record data from more than 139 million patients across 110 healthcare organizations (HCOs) at the time of query (Fig. 1). Standardized coding systems included ATC codes for medication classes, ICD-10-CM for diagnoses, CPT codes for procedures, and RxNorm for individual medications (Appendix Table). This study was exempt from institutional review board oversight given the de-identified nature of the data.Fig. 1Study Design and Cohort Selection Flow Diagram. Flow diagram illustrating cohort selection from the TriNetX Analytics Network. Adult patients (18–90 years) with obesity and no diabetes were identified. Cohort 1 included patients initiating concurrent GLP-1 receptor agonist (GLP-1RA) and SGLT2 inhibitor therapy, while Cohort 2 included patients receiving GLP-1RA alone. After applying inclusion and exclusion criteria, 1:1 propensity score matching yielded 26,106 patients per group. ### Study Design

We conducted a propensity score–matched retrospective cohort study using an incident user design to evaluate arrhythmia outcomes following first documented concurrent use of GLP-1 receptor agonists (GLP-1RA) and SGLT2 inhibitors (SGLT2i), compared with GLP-1RA use alone. GLP-1RA prescriptions were mostly Semaglutide (71.9%), Dulaglutide (27.0%), Liraglutide (16.2%), Exenatide (5.0%), Lexisenatide (1.0%). SGLT2i prescriptions comprised of Empagliflozin (67.2%), Dapagliflozin (37.2%), Canagliflozin (8.7%), Ertugliflozin (1.4%), and Bexagliflozin (0.1%). The index event was defined as the first recorded concurrent exposure to both GLP-1RA and SGLT2i on or after January 1, 2018, for Cohort 1, or the first recorded GLP-1RA exposure without SGLT2i on or after January 1, 2018, for Cohort 2. Outcomes were assessed beginning 1 day after the index event across six pre-specified follow-up windows: 6 months (180 days), 12 months (365 days), 18 months (540 days), 2 years (730 days), 5 years (1825 days; primary analysis), and 8 years (2920 days).

### Study population

Cohort 1 (GLP-1RA + SGLT2i) comprised adults aged 18–90 years with obesity (BMI ≥30 kg/m2 or ICD-10 diagnosis of obesity) who received both a GLP-1RA and an SGLT2 inhibitor on or after January 1, 2018, and had no diagnosis of type 1 diabetes, type 2 diabetes, other specified diabetes mellitus, or gestational diabetes. Cohort 2 (GLP-1RA Only) comprised patients meeting identical obesity criteria who received a GLP-1RA but had no concurrent or prior SGLT2i exposure. The pre-matching cohort sizes were 27,675 (GLP-1RA + SGLT2i) and 542,465 (GLP-1RA Only); after 1:1 propensity score matching, each cohort comprised 26,106 patients (Fig. 1).

### Outcomes

Four incident arrhythmia outcomes were evaluated [1]: composite arrhythmia, defined as new-onset atrial fibrillation or flutter, ventricular tachycardia, or ventricular fibrillation [2]; atrial fibrillation and flutter [3]; ventricular tachycardia; and [4] ventricular fibrillation. Ventricular fibrillation was not assessed in the 6-month analysis, as the occurrence was too small to generate a result. All outcomes were treated as incident events; patients with the respective outcome documented before the index event were excluded from each specific outcome analysis to ensure valid at-risk denominators.

### Propensity score matching

Propensity scores were estimated using a comprehensive set of baseline covariates documented before the index event, including age at index event, current age, sex, race and ethnicity, baseline diagnoses, a surgical procedure, and baseline medications (see Table 1 for the full covariate list; codes are listed in the Appendix Table). The same matched cohorts were used across all six follow-up windows. Patients were matched 1:1 using nearest-neighbor matching without replacement. Post-matching cohorts demonstrated good balance across all variables.

### Statistical analysis

Clinical outcomes were evaluated using risk-based analyses. For each outcome, the proportion of patients with the event was calculated per cohort. The odds ratio (OR) with 95% confidence interval was estimated, and p-values were derived using z-tests. All tests were two-sided; p < 0.05 was considered statistically significant. The 5-year window constitutes the primary analysis. All other windows are pre-specified secondary analyses reported in the supplementary table. Analyses were performed using the built-in analytical tools of the TriNetX Analytics Platform. This study was designed and reported in accordance with the STROBE guidelines for observational research.

## Results

### Primary analysis (5-year follow-up)

Baseline Cohort Characteristics. After 1:1 propensity score matching, both cohorts comprised 26,106 patients each. Before matching, the GLP-1RA + SGLT2i cohort was substantially older (mean age at index 58.3 ± 12.7 vs. 46.9 ± 14.4 years; SMD 0.835), predominantly male (46.3% vs. 24.6%; SMD 0.465), and carried a markedly higher burden of cardiovascular comorbidities, including heart failure (23.4% vs. 2.1%; SMD 0.673), chronic ischemic heart disease (15.4% vs. 5.0%; SMD 0.350), chronic kidney disease (9.8% vs. 2.6%; SMD 0.300), and secondary pulmonary hypertension (6.3% vs. 0.9%; SMD 0.297), consistent with the preferential prescribing of SGLT2i in higher-risk patients and for indications such as heart failure and prevention of chronic kidney disease progression. Following propensity score matching on all listed covariates, substantial improvement in baseline balance was achieved across demographic characteristics, comorbidities, and baseline medications. Most standardized mean differences were below 0.10 (Table 1).

Atrial Fibrillation/Flutter: Atrial fibrillation/flutter at 5 years occurred in 430 of 23,437 eligible GLP-1RA + SGLT2i patients (1.8%) versus 526 of 23,629 GLP-1RA-only patients (2.2%), representing 17.9% lower odds in the combination group (OR 0.821, 95% CI 0.722–0.934; p = 0.003) (Table 2, Fig. 2).

Ventricular Tachycardia: Ventricular tachycardia at 5 years occurred in 160 of 25,133 eligible GLP-1RA + SGLT2i patients (0.6%) versus 137 of 25,499 GLP-1RA-only patients (0.5%), with no statistically significant difference in odds between groups (OR 1.186, 95% CI 0.943–1.491; p = 0.143) (Table 2, Fig. 2).

Ventricular Fibrillation: Ventricular fibrillation at 5 years occurred in 26 of 25,937 eligible GLP-1RA + SGLT2i patients (0.1%) versus 20 of 26,013 GLP-1RA-only patients (0.1%), with no statistically significant difference in odds (OR 1.304, 95% CI 0.728–2.337; p = 0.371) (Table 2, Fig. 2).

Across follow-up windows, Atrial fibrillation/flutter odds with combination therapy trended as follows: OR 0.986(0.800-1.214) at 6 months, OR 0.916(0.778-1.077) at 12 months, OR 0.851(0.734-0.986) at 18 months, OR 0.835(0.726-0.961) at 24 months, OR 0.821(0.722-0.934) at 60 months, and OR 0.801(0.706-0.910) at 96 months. The combination therapy resulted in a lower occurrence of Atrial fibrillation/flutter starting as early as 18 months and persisted to 96 months (Table 3, Fig. 3).

Ventricular tachycardia was higher in the combination therapy group from 6 months to 24 months, OR 1.625(1.119–2.359) at 6 months, OR 1.472(1.102–1.965) at 12 months, OR 1.429 (1.092–1.871) at 18 months, and OR 1.336(1.043–1.712) at 24 months. At 60 and 96 months, there was no difference between the two groups, OR 1.186(0.943–1.491) at 60 months and OR 1.176 (0.937–1.477) at 96 months (Table 3, Fig. 3).

Ventricular fibrillation was not significant across all study periods between the 2 groups. OR 1.588 (0.771–3.273) at 12 months, OR 1.852 (0.943–3.639) at 18 months, OR 1.505 (0.799–2.834) at 24 months, OR 1.304 (0.728–2.337) at 60 months, OR 1.304 (0.728–2.337) at 96 months (Table 3, Fig. 3).

## Discussion

In this large real-world study of non-diabetic obese patients, combination therapy with GLP-1 RA and SGLT2i was associated with 17.5% lower odds of composite arrhythmia compared with GLP-1RA alone at 60 months. This benefit was evident as early as 24 months and persisted through 96 months. The composite arrhythmia endpoint was selected a priori to capture the overall burden of clinically relevant cardiac rhythm disturbances and to provide a comprehensive assessment of the arrhythmic effects of combination GLP-1RA and SGLT2i therapy. Given the relatively low incidence of individual ventricular arrhythmias, particularly ventricular fibrillation, the use of a composite endpoint increased statistical power while allowing evaluation of both atrial and ventricular rhythm outcomes. Importantly, analysis of the individual components demonstrated that the observed reduction in the composite endpoint was driven predominantly by decreases in atrial fibrillation and atrial flutter, which were 17.9% lower in the combination group at 60 months. These findings suggest that combination therapy may reduce overall arrhythmia burden, largely through favorable effects on atrial arrhythmias.

Our findings are consistent with prior studies evaluating the arrhythmic effects of SGLT2i. Multiple meta-analyses and real-world studies have shown that SGLT2i are associated with a reduction in atrial fibrillation and flutter, with relatively neutral effects on ventricular arrhythmias [[15], [16], [17], [18]]. Proposed mechanisms include improved cardiac loading conditions, reduced atrial stretch, and attenuation of inflammation and fibrosis [21,22]. In contrast, GLP-1 RAs have demonstrated a generally neutral to modestly favorable arrhythmia profile, with meta-analyses showing no increased risk of atrial or ventricular arrhythmias and some studies suggesting reductions in incident atrial fibrillation, particularly with semaglutide [[11], [12], [13], [14]]. Taken together, the reduction in atrial arrhythmias observed in our study is likely driven by the addition of SGLT2 inhibition, with potential complementary effects from GLP-1RA.

An interesting finding of our study is the time-dependent pattern observed in ventricular arrhythmias. We noted a higher incidence of VT in the combination group during early follow-up (6, 12, 18, and 24 months). However, this difference was not sustained and became similar between groups at longer follow-up (60 and 96 months). This may suggest that over time, the beneficial effects of both drug classes may become more prominent. Weight loss, improved hemodynamics, and reduced myocardial stress may contribute to a more stable cardiac substrate, which could explain the reduction in atrial arrhythmias and the normalization of VT risk [21,23]. Other factors may explain this observation. Residual confounding and indication bias remain possible despite robust propensity score matching, as patients selected for combination therapy may have had higher cardiometabolic risk, or a greater burden of subclinical cardiovascular disease that was not fully captured by available covariates. In addition, physiologic effects associated with SGLT2i therapy, including osmotic diuresis, transient volume contraction, and alterations in electrolyte homeostasis, could theoretically influence ventricular arrhythmogenicity in susceptible individuals, although prior randomized trials and meta-analyses have generally not demonstrated an increased long-term risk of ventricular arrhythmias with SGLT2 inhibitors [13,24]. Unmeasured arrhythmogenic substrates, such as myocardial fibrosis, occult cardiomyopathy, autonomic dysfunction, or baseline ventricular ectopy burden, may have also contributed.

Alternative epidemiologic explanations should also be considered. Because continuous medication exposure and treatment persistence could not be verified throughout follow-up, the observed convergence of VT risk over time may reflect survivor or attrition bias, whereby patients experiencing early adverse events, treatment discontinuation, or loss to follow-up were less likely to contribute data at later time points, rather than a true attenuation of arrhythmic risk. Importantly, the early increase in VT was not accompanied by a corresponding increase in ventricular fibrillation or other malignant ventricular arrhythmias, and the observed risk gradually converged over time, suggesting that the finding may reflect transient patient-selection factors or short-term physiologic adaptations rather than a persistent proarrhythmic effect of combination therapy. Nevertheless, because laboratory values, imaging data, electrocardiographic parameters, and rhythm-monitoring information were unavailable, the mechanism underlying this early VT increase could not be directly assessed and warrants further investigation in prospective studies.

Ventricular fibrillation rates remained similar between groups throughout the follow-up period, further supporting the overall electrophysiologic safety of combination therapy. Prior studies of both GLP-1RAs and SGLT2i have similarly shown no consistent increase in malignant ventricular arrhythmias or sudden cardiac death, reinforcing the safety of these agents from a ventricular arrhythmia standpoint [13,15].

This study is particularly important because it focuses on a non-diabetic obese population, where data is limited. Most prior studies evaluating GLP-1RAs and SGLT2i have been conducted in patients with diabetes, making it difficult to separate medication effects from the underlying metabolic disease [25,26]. By examining a non-diabetic cohort, our study provides clearer insight into the direct electrophysiologic effects of these therapies. Furthermore, this analysis represents one of the first large-scale evaluations of arrhythmia outcomes with combination GLP-1RA and SGLT2i therapy, addressing an important gap in the literature and highlighting the importance of time-dependent effects in arrhythmia risk assessment.

### Limitations

This study is limited by its retrospective design and the potential for residual confounding despite robust propensity score matching. Most standardized mean differences were reduced to below 0.10 after matching; however, modest residual imbalance remained for age-related variables, including age at index (SMD 0.115) and current age (SMD 0.130). The absolute difference in age between matched cohorts was relatively small (approximately 1.5 years), and balance was achieved across a broad range of cardiovascular comorbidities, medications, and other arrhythmia-related risk factors. Aldosterone antagonist and Sacubitril-valsartan also remained slightly imbalanced after propensity score matching which could theoretically skew results in favor of the combination group who may be on SGLT2i for heart failure. Medication exposure was defined using EHR documentation of prescriptions or medication use, which may not reliably capture actual adherence, persistence, dose, or treatment duration. This is particularly relevant because differential non-adherence between groups could bias the observed association. For example, lower adherence to either GLP-1RA or SGLT2i therapy in the combination group would likely dilute any true treatment effect, whereas preferential continuation among patients who tolerated and benefited from therapy could overestimate the observed benefit. In addition, treatment discontinuation, delayed initiation, or intermittent use could not be fully assessed, limiting our ability to determine whether arrhythmia reduction was related to sustained combination therapy. Arrhythmia outcomes were identified using diagnostic codes and may be subject to misclassification or under-ascertainment, particularly for subclinical events. Important clinical variables, including weight trajectory, imaging findings, laboratory data, medication dose, rhythm monitoring intensity, and arrhythmia burden, were not available.

## Conclusion

In non-diabetic obese patients, combination therapy with GLP-1RA and SGLT2i was associated with a lower risk of composite arrhythmia, driven primarily by a reduction in atrial arrhythmias, without a sustained increase in ventricular arrhythmias. Although a transient early increase in ventricular tachycardia was observed, this difference diminished over time. These findings may suggest a favorable long-term electrophysiologic profile of combination therapy and highlight the importance of time-dependent analysis. Prospective studies are needed to confirm these results.
